description: Hello! I am a 4th-year CS student bridging space medicine and engineering. I build physics-informed ML, computer vision, and offline clinical RAG platforms to safeguard human health in deep space. While this is my first NASA Space Apps, as a solo dev, I aim to prove that when scientific computing meets AI, we can expand the boundaries of human exploration while keeping astronauts safe on the final frontier.
summary:
TALA (Twin-based Astronaut Life Analytics) is an exploratory astronaut exercise-monitoring platform designed to support the understanding of movement and wellness in spaceflight environments. It combines computer vision, OpenSim-based kinematic reconstruction, biomechanical and movement analysis, and NASA literature-grounded artificial intelligence.

Using exercise video, TALA extracts human pose landmarks and uses them to inform a musculoskeletal model-based reconstruction. It then analyzes movement characteristics, estimates center-of-mass behavior, and compares gravitational potential energy under different gravity environments. A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) component connects the analytical outputs with relevant NASA human-health and spaceflight literature, providing evidence-grounded context.

We developed a research-oriented Python backend and a deployed interactive frontend MVP that demonstrates the platform's intended user experience using precomputed data. TALA explores how computer vision, biomechanical modeling, and NASA research can be brought together to make astronaut exercise observations more interpretable and accessible, particularly in the context of long-duration space missions.
details:
TALA (Twin-based Astronaut Life Analytics) explores how computer vision, musculoskeletal modeling, and artificial intelligence can be integrated to support astronaut exercise monitoring and movement analysis. Its goal is to make exercise-related observations more interpretable by connecting visual movement data with biomechanical analysis and relevant NASA research.

How It Works

TALA follows a four-stage backend workflow:

  1. Computer Vision: Uses MediaPipe Pose Landmarker to extract body landmarks from astronaut exercise footage.
  2. Kinematic Reconstruction: Maps the extracted observations to an OpenSim musculoskeletal model and applies inverse kinematics to estimate model-constrained joint movement.
  3. Biomechanical and Movement Analysis: Examines movement phases, repetitions, joint-coordinate observations, and whole-body center-of-mass behavior. It also compares gravitational potential energy along the same reconstructed movement trajectory under Earth, lunar, Martian, and microgravity conditions.
  4. NASA Literature-Grounded AI: Uses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to retrieve information from NASA human-health and spaceflight documents and generate contextual explanations related to the analytical results.

The project also includes a deployed interactive frontend MVP that demonstrates the intended user experience through precomputed data from the research workflow. The frontend is a demonstration prototype rather than a live integration with the backend.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Astronauts experience unique challenges during spaceflight, including changes in gravitational loading and physiological deconditioning. Exercise is an important countermeasure, but interpreting movement observations alongside relevant research can be challenging.

TALA explores a way to bring these different sources of information together. Its intended impact is to support more accessible interpretation of exercise movement, provide context from established NASA literature, and demonstrate a potential foundation for future astronaut health and exercise-support systems.

Technologies and Tools

The backend was developed primarily in Python 3.11, using:

  • MediaPipe Pose Landmarker for computer-vision-based pose estimation.
  • OpenSim for musculoskeletal modeling and inverse kinematics.
  • NumPy and Pandas for numerical processing and data analysis.
  • Ollama with Qwen3 Embedding 0.6B for local document and query embeddings.
  • ChromaDB for vector storage and semantic retrieval.
  • Google Gemini for retrieval-grounded natural-language generation.
  • Pytest for automated testing.

The project also uses a web-based frontend prototype, deployed separately from the research backend.

Creativity and Design Considerations

TALA's creative approach is its integration of visual movement analysis, physics-based musculoskeletal modeling, and NASA-document retrieval within one exploratory workflow. Rather than treating AI as the sole source of analysis, it separates numerical computation from language generation: biomechanical quantities are calculated by dedicated analytical components, while the RAG system provides supporting literature context.

During development, we considered scientific defensibility, limited development time, reproducibility, computational constraints, data availability, and the risks of interpreting monocular video as ground-truth three-dimensional motion. We therefore kept the scope focused on kinematic reconstruction and exploratory movement analysis, clearly distinguishing model-derived estimates from direct measurements.

TALA is not a clinically validated diagnostic system. It is a research prototype demonstrating how these technologies could contribute to future tools for understanding astronaut exercise and supporting human health during space exploration.
